title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Four Pillars, One Engine—Inside Lilly's Clinical Portfolio

epigraph.quote: We are focused on solving the most serious and challenging diseases facing humanity, where scientific breakthroughs can change the standard of care.
epigraph.author: David A. Ricks, Chair & CEO, Eli Lilly

web_blocks.html: Eli Lilly runs one main business: human drugs. It groups those drugs into four pillars: Metabolic Care, Oncology, Immunology, and Neuroscience. In FY2025, global sales jumped 44.7% YoY to $65,179 million, up from $45,043 million in FY2024 and $34,124 million in FY2023. By Q3 2026, quarterly sales hit $24,400 million (+39% YoY). That pace keeps Lilly on track for its raised FY2026 sales goal of $91.0 billion to $92.0 billion.

Metabolic Care leads the top line. Mounjaro ($22,965M) and Zepbound ($13,542M) together made up 56.0% of FY2025 sales. Still, Lilly's other pillars add broad balance, high margins, and steady pipeline options. Verzenio ($5,723M in FY2025) anchors Oncology, while Taltz ($3,910M), Ebglyss, and Omvoh drive Immunology. In Neuroscience, Kisunla (donanemab) is building a disease-slowing foothold alongside Emgality.

web_blocks.html: To see how Lilly earns its profits, look at one real-world case in each of its four pillars:

web_blocks.title: 1. Cardiometabolic Health (Diabetes & Obesity): Mounjaro, Zepbound & Foundayo
paragraphs: Patient & Problem: A 48-year-old patient has Class II obesity (BMI 36) plus sleep apnea or Type 2 diabetes. Diet, exercise, and older pills have failed, leaving high heart and metabolic risk.

Prescriber & Product: A doctor prescribes weekly Zepbound (tirzepatide) by auto-injector pen. Since April 2026, patients who prefer a pill can take once-daily Foundayo (orforglipron) with no food or water timing rules.

Manufacturing & Delivery: Tirzepatide needs complex peptide synthesis and sterile fill-finish into single-dose pens or KwikPens. Wholesalers like McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health ship it cold-chain, or LillyDirect delivers straight to homes. Foundayo uses standard tablet plants, skipping cold storage.
Pricing & Reimbursement: Commercial plans cover ~55–65% of eligible lives after prior checks and 35–55% PBM rebates. Uninsured or denied patients often use LillyDirect cash tiers at $349–$499/month.

web_blocks.title: 2. Oncology: Verzenio & Jaypirca
paragraphs: Patient & Problem: A 54-year-old woman diagnosed with node-positive, HR-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer faces a 20–30% risk of distant recurrence after surgery and chemotherapy.

Prescriber & Product: A medical oncologist prescribes Verzenio (abemaciclib) 150 mg twice-daily oral tablets for two years alongside endocrine therapy (adjuvant setting), where Verzenio is the only CDK4/6 inhibitor with proven overall survival and invasive disease-free survival benefit in high-risk early disease. In relapsed mantle cell lymphoma or CLL, hematologists similarly prescribe Lilly's non-covalent BTK inhibitor Jaypirca (pirtobrutinib).

Manufacturing & Delivery: Oral small-molecule tablets manufactured at Lilly's global oral solid-dose facilities and dispensed through specialty pharmacies (e.g., CVS Specialty, Accredo) with monthly adherence monitoring.

Pricing & Reimbursement: High-value oncology biologics/orals carry strong commercial and Medicare Part D coverage with minimal formulary exclusion because clinical guidelines (NCCN Category 1) mandate access; net realization is governed by statutory 340B/Medicaid/Medicare Part D redesign discounts rather than aggressive PBM tiering.

web_blocks.title: 3. Immunology: Taltz, Ebglyss & Omvoh
paragraphs: Patient & Problem: A 32-year-old adult with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (eczema) or ulcerative colitis experiences debilitating flares, sleep loss, and inadequate relief from topical steroids or legacy anti-TNF biologics.

Prescriber & Product: A dermatologist prescribes Ebglyss (lebrikizumab, an IL-13 monoclonal antibody) with monthly maintenance dosing after induction, or a gastroenterologist prescribes Omvoh (mirikizumab, an IL-23p19 antagonist) for ulcerative colitis/Crohn's disease; in plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, Taltz (ixekizumab) remains a $3.9B+ workhorse.

Manufacturing & Delivery: Mammalian cell-culture bioreactor fermentation (CHO cells) producing monoclonal antibodies, purified and filled into prefilled syringes/auto-injectors, delivered via specialty pharmacies with nurse-ambassador injection training.

Pricing & Reimbursement: Immunology is fiercely competitive (against Dupixent, Skyrizi, and Rinvoq), meaning PBMs demand substantial rebates and step-therapy ('fail-first' on older agents) for preferred formulary placement.

web_blocks.title: 4. Neuroscience: Kisunla (Donanemab) & Emgality
paragraphs: Patient & Problem: A 71-year-old patient with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or mild dementia due to confirmed amyloid-beta pathology faces irreversible cognitive decline.

Prescriber & Product: A neurologist confirms amyloid plaque via PET scan or CSF/blood biomarker, orders baseline brain MRI to screen for ARIA risk, and prescribes Kisunla (donanemab-azbt), an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody.

Manufacturing & Delivery: Biologic IV infusion administered every four weeks at hospital outpatient or freestanding infusion centers; uniquely, Kisunla's label allows finite-duration dosing—stopping therapy once amyloid plaques are cleared on follow-up PET.

Pricing & Reimbursement: Reimbursed primarily under Medicare Part B (medical benefit, ASP + 6% framework) with registry participation; commercial uptake has scaled steadily ($109M in Q4 2025, +54% QoQ) as infusion infrastructure and diagnostic PET capacity expand.

web_blocks.html: Regional and channel mix also shape Lilly's sales quality. In FY2025, Mounjaro earned $13,651 million in the U.S. and $9,315 million abroad (40.6% ex-U.S.). That shows strong uptake across Europe, Japan, and the Middle East. By contrast, Zepbound's $13,542 million in FY2025 sales was 99.6% U.S. ($13,484 million U.S. vs. $58 million ex-U.S.). Overseas obesity payers have moved slowly, though multi-dose KwikPens are now rolling out.

Across all four pillars, strong trial data backs Lilly's formulary edge. In metabolic care, SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-OSA showed 21%–22% mean weight loss and sleep-apnea relief for tirzepatide. Retatrutide's Phase 3 TRIUMPH trials also hit up to ~28% weight loss. In cancer, monarchE proved Verzenio cuts recurrence and boosts survival in high-risk early breast cancer. In brain health, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 showed Kisunla slowed early Alzheimer's decline by 35% with finite dosing.

Lilly's older drugs also form a cash bridge while new launches scale. Trulicity ($4,276 million in FY2025), Jardiance ($3,260 million partner sales), Humalog, and Cyramza lead this group. Management guides doctors to move diabetes patients from Trulicity to Mounjaro. That keeps patients inside Lilly's ecosystem instead of losing them to rival GLP-1 brands.

Q3 2026 filings sharpen two portfolio risks. First, tirzepatide concentration climbed rather than eased: Mounjaro ($10,723 million) and Zepbound ($5,352 million) generated $16,075 million in Q3 2026—65.9% of total revenue ($24,397 million)—and $43,768 million (65.2%) across 9M 2026. Second, regulatory pricing pressure now reaches beyond diabetes: under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), HHS selected Jardiance (66% discount effective 2026, with no further Boehringer Ingelheim sales-based milestones remaining after $910 million in 9M 2026) and in January 2026 selected both Trulicity ($4,276 million FY2025) and Verzenio ($5,723 million FY2025)—15.4% of FY2025 revenue—for Medicare price-setting effective 2028.

book_paragraphs: When you and I look at Eli Lilly's income statement today, it is tempting to reduce the entire company to two words: Mounjaro and Zepbound. After all, those two tirzepatide brands generated $36.5 billion in FY2025—56% of Lilly's $65.2 billion top line—and topped $16 billion in the third quarter of 2026 alone. But if we stop there, we miss how the rest of Lilly's four-pillar engine works, and why its diversification in oncology, immunology, and neuroscience matters to the durability of the enterprise.

Unlike a conglomerate with unrelated divisions, Lilly operates as a single, integrated human pharmaceuticals machine organized around four therapeutic areas. Each area has its own biological modality, manufacturing footprint, prescriber base, and payer economics. Let's walk through all four from the patient's perspective all the way back to the factory floor and the reimbursement check.

As of the Q3 2026 10-Q, two portfolio realities require sharper underwriting. First, tirzepatide concentration rose from 56.0% in FY2025 to 65.9% of Q3 2026 revenue ($16,075 million of $24,397 million), even as Foundayo ($184 million in Q3 2026), Ebglyss ($202 million), and Kisunla ($193 million) scaled rapidly. Second, in January 2026 HHS selected both Trulicity and Verzenio (together 15.4% of FY2025 revenue) for IRA Medicare price negotiation effective 2028, following Jardiance's 66% Medicare discount effective 2026 and the completion of all remaining Jardiance sales-based milestones.

book_subsections.title: Pillar 1: Cardiometabolic Health — From Weekly Pens to Daily Pills
paragraphs: Picture a 48-year-old patient with obesity and sleep apnea sitting in a primary-care exam room. For decades, medicine offered little more than lifestyle lectures and bariatric surgery. Today, that physician writes a prescription for Zepbound (tirzepatide). Behind that prescription sits an extraordinary industrial chain: solid-phase peptide synthesis at chemical API plants, sterile fill-finish into precision auto-injector pens, and cold-chain distribution through wholesalers or straight to the patient's doorstep via LillyDirect.

And as of April 2026, that same physician has an entirely different option for the needle-averse patient: Foundayo (orforglipron), Lilly's FDA-approved oral small-molecule GLP-1 pill. Unlike peptide injectables, Foundayo requires no refrigeration and no fasting window—expanding the addressable market into primary care and international geographies where cold-chain logistics are scarce.

book_subsections.title: Pillars 2, 3, and 4: Oncology, Immunology, and Neuroscience
paragraphs: Step into an oncology clinic and you see Lilly's second pillar in action. Verzenio, a $5.7 billion oral CDK4/6 inhibitor, is prescribed for two years to high-risk early breast cancer patients to prevent recurrence—a sticky, guideline-mandated specialty business with far less PBM rebate friction than primary care. Alongside it, Jaypirca is carving out a niche in blood cancers for patients who relapse on older BTK inhibitors.

In immunology, Lilly's $3.9 billion Taltz franchise is now flanked by two fast-growing monoclonal antibodies: Ebglyss for eczema and Omvoh for inflammatory bowel disease. Here, the battle is fought on PBM formularies, where biologics compete head-to-head on net price and dosing convenience. Finally, in neuroscience, Kisunla (donanemab) represents one of the hardest problems in medicine: clearing amyloid plaques in early Alzheimer's disease, with a finite-duration dosing protocol that lets patients stop monthly IV infusions once plaques clear.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Concentration Risk vs. Platform Depth
callouts.text: Yes, tirzepatide is 56% of revenue—a level of concentration that demands respect. Yet unlike a one-trick biotech, Lilly's non-incretin portfolio already exceeds $28 billion in annualized revenue across six $3B+ brands and three newly launched specialty biologics. The incretin cash flow is funding the next decade of oncology, immunology, and neuroscience.

book_subsections.title: Geographic Asymmetry: Why Zepbound Is Still Mostly a U.S. Story
paragraphs: Here is a detail buried in Note 2 of Lilly's FY2025 10-K that most casual observers miss: Mounjaro is already a truly global blockbuster, with $9.3 billion—over 40% of its $23.0 billion revenue—coming from outside the United States. Zepbound, by contrast, generated $13.48 billion in the U.S. and just $58 million internationally in 2025. Why the massive gap?

Outside the United States, single-payer health systems in Europe and Asia have been slow to reimburse injectable obesity drugs, treating weight management as a lifestyle expense rather than a cardiovascular intervention. That is beginning to change as outcomes data in heart failure, sleep apnea, and MASH accumulate—and as Lilly rolls out multi-dose KwikPens and oral Foundayo, which eliminates cold-chain refrigeration. For you and I, that geographic asymmetry means international obesity represents a multi-year volume runway that has barely started.

book_subsections.title: How Each Modality Dictates Margin and Stickiness
paragraphs: When we compare Lilly's four pillars side by side, notice how the underlying biology dictates the business model. Peptide injectables like Mounjaro and Zepbound require complex chemical synthesis and sterile pen assembly, creating high physical barriers to entry. Oral small molecules like Verzenio, Jaypirca, and Foundayo use traditional chemical tableting—cheaper to manufacture, easier to ship globally, and free of cold-chain constraints. Monoclonal antibodies like Taltz, Ebglyss, Omvoh, and Kisunla rely on mammalian cell-culture bioreactors, where biosimilar entrants face steeper FDA clinical-equivalence hurdles than simple small-molecule generics.

Together, those three modalities—peptides, small molecules, and biologics—give Lilly a balanced technological toolkit. Rather than betting the company on a single manufacturing platform, Lilly matches the modality to the disease: oral pills where daily convenience wins primary care, sterile pens where dual- and triple-receptor potency is unmatched, and targeted antibodies where immune or amyloid specificity is required.

book_subsections.title: Why Clinical Outcomes Labels Lock In Payers
paragraphs: In obesity and diabetes, payers initially resisted covering expensive incretin therapies, arguing that weight loss was cosmetic. Lilly's clinical strategy systematically dismantled that objection by running large, expensive outcomes trials across adjacent organ systems: obstructive sleep apnea, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease, and metabolic liver disease (MASH).

Every time an outcomes trial proves that tirzepatide reduces hospitalizations, sleep-apnea events, or cardiovascular mortality, commercial insurers and government payers lose their justification for blanket exclusions. For Verzenio in breast cancer, Kisunla in Alzheimer's, and Omvoh in ulcerative colitis, the same principle applies: hard clinical endpoints—overall survival, amyloid plaque clearance, endoscopic remission—are what turn a new drug from a discretionary expense into a standard-of-care necessity.

book_subsections.title: The Emerging Wave: Ebglyss, Omvoh, Jaypirca, and Kisunla
paragraphs: Because Mounjaro and Zepbound dominate the headlines, it is easy to overlook the four specialty launches quietly compounding underneath: Ebglyss ($134 million in Q4 2025, +25% sequential U.S. prescription growth), Kisunla ($109 million in Q4 2025, +54% QoQ), Omvoh ($88 million in Q4 2025, +22% sequential U.S. TRx), and Jaypirca in blood cancers. Individually, each is still small relative to a $65 billion top line; collectively, they represent Lilly's post-2030 diversification engine.

book_subsections.title: Why Physician Detailing Still Matters in Specialty Care
paragraphs: Notice one more thread running through all four pillars: Lilly's commercial force does not just drop off samples at primary-care offices. In oncology, immunology, and Alzheimer's neurology, Lilly's medical science liaisons work directly with academic cancer centers, infusion clinics, and specialty pharmacies to navigate complex biomarker testing, MRI safety monitoring, and prior-authorization paperwork.

That clinical-support infrastructure is expensive—it sits inside Lilly's $11.09 billion marketing, selling, and administrative line—but it creates real switching costs. Once an oncology practice integrates Verzenio into its adjuvant breast cancer pathway, or a neurology center builds a PET-and-infusion workflow around Kisunla, a challenger molecule needs a decisive clinical advantage, not a marginal rebate, to displace it.

book_subsections.title: Why Non-Incretin Franchises Still Anchor the Portfolio
paragraphs: While Mounjaro and Zepbound dominate headlines, investors should not overlook the durability of Lillys non-incretin pillars. Verzenio generated $5.72 billion in FY2025 high-risk early breast cancer sales with strong patent protection into the 2030s, while Taltz ($3.91 billion) and newly launched Ebglyss anchor a growing immunology franchise.

Meanwhile, Kisunla in early symptomatic Alzheimer disease and Jaypirca in oncology provide long-dated optionality that diversifies Lilly beyond metabolic medicine. Together, these non-incretin businesses contribute roughly $28.7 billion in annual high-margin revenue and fund continuous R&D.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Follow the Payer, Not Just the Molecule
book_callouts.text: Notice how differently each pillar gets paid: Medicare Part B for infused Kisunla, specialty pharmacy and NCCN-protected Part D for Verzenio, rebated commercial formularies for Ebglyss, and hybrid PBM plus cash-pay LillyDirect for Zepbound and Foundayo. Understanding those four reimbursement pipes is essential before we touch a single valuation multiple.
